task_brief: This is day 4 of "Pictures, Sounds, and Simple Data". That is unit 5 in grade 3. Today is a build and test about comparing two data sets. It takes about 40–60 minutes. It is one day's work, not the whole unit project. Your unit is working toward this: Collect a small set of data and create a simple picture graph with a short conclusion. Today helps by working on comparing two data sets. Your unit also covers sorting and counting objects, simple picture graphs, choosing a picture that fits, and comparing two data sets. Today adds real evidence toward your unit project.
primary_task: Build something that solves a real need in your unit "Pictures, Sounds, and Simple Data". Build it around what today covers: comparing two data sets. First write what it must do. Write it so you can check it later. Then build it. Test it three ways: a normal case, a tricky case, and one you think will break it. Write down what happened each time. Fix anything that failed. Test again. Turn in the thing you built, your test notes, and one idea you tried but did not use. Keep today's work tied to your unit. Today is about comparing two data sets. It is part of "Pictures, Sounds, and Simple Data". Later days in this unit cover other things, like sorting and counting objects. Before you stop, do this check: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about comparing two data sets; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. In grade 3 you need one clear try with a grown-up nearby. Say or write your reason in a sentence or two. Drawings, objects, or spoken answers are all fine.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.

Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
task_accessibility_provisions: You can do this with the keyboard only, no mouse needed. Text can be made bigger, and you may do it on paper instead of a screen.
This work takes more than one sitting. Ask for a simple checklist with dates so you know what to do next. Keeping track is not part of your grade.
You can take a break, stretch, or come back to this later. That does not lower your score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Never require a real password, private message, precise location, account credential, API key, or identifiable image.
Use only fictional or sandboxed systems, accounts, and data; never probe, exploit, or attempt to access a real external system.

remediation: Reteaching for comparing two data sets follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for comparing two data sets, model it with a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the process for comparing two data sets works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of comparing two data sets, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking comparing two data sets mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply comparing two data sets under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on comparing two data sets rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
